title: Does Marriage Matter More Than We Thought? Challenging the Selection Narrative arrative
author: Harry Benson
summary: Harry Benson, research director of the UK Marriage Foundation, summarises his PhD thesis challenging the 'selection' consensus that married parents stay together only because stable people are the ones who marry. He replicated the influential UK Institute for Fiscal Studies analyses of the Millennium Cohort Study, then changed two things: he retained the roughly one quarter of families dropped for missing data, who were disproportionately unmarried or later separated, and he compared parents who eventually married over 14 years with those who never did, rather than 'married at birth' with 'not yet married'. With these changes selection explained only about half or less of the difference in family stability, and marriage kept a substantial independent association after 27 controls. Benson argues researchers have been better at explaining why marriage might not matter than why it does, and he points to psychological mechanisms (deciding versus sliding, costly public signalling and cognitive consistency) by which marriage may actually create commitment.
points: Excluding families with missing data removed a disproportionately unstable quarter of the sample and biased earlier studies toward finding that marriage made no difference.
Treating parents who marry within a few years as 'unmarried' understates the long-term link between marriage and stability.
With both corrections, selection explains only about half or less of the stability gap and marriage retains a substantial independent association.
Headline summaries rarely mention methodological choices, so conventional wisdom can rest on regression decisions most readers never see.
Psychology offers mechanisms, such as signal theory and cognitive consistency, for marriage creating commitment rather than merely reflecting it.
quotes: Instead of selection explaining almost all the difference in family stability, it explained only about half.

Missing data are rarely random. Families with incomplete information are often those experiencing greater instability, financial hardship, or relationship stress. Excluding them risks producing biased estimates.

If the research question is whether marriage contributes to family stability over childhood, comparing "married" with "not yet married" is likely to understate the long-term association between marriage and stability.

This omission matters because relatively few readers study regression tables. Policymakers and journalists generally absorb the headline conclusions, and over time, those conclusions become conventional wisdom.
Cognitive consistency theory suggests that once people publicly commit themselves to a lifelong relationship, they become motivated to behave consistently with that commitment.
In other words, marriage may not simply reflect commitment. It may also help create it.
Family researchers have become exceptionally good at explaining why marriage might not matter. They have devoted much less attention to understanding why it does.
